FAA Expands AI Advice to Manage Air Traffic Congestion Across Entire US Airspace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

FAA Expands AI Advice to Manage Air Traffic Congestion Across Entire US Airspace 2
			
		 	
				The FAA is expanding its $875 million AI-powered SMART system to all 22 U.S. air traffic control centers across the country. Since being implemented over Washington, DC, on September 21, the system has helped reroute 180 flights, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight. Ars Technica reports:  The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about "weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics" to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft. However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency. Furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system "cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft," the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. Local air traffic controllers can decide whether or not to accept the SMART system recommendations.
[...] Following the initial deployment in airspace above DC, the FAA expanded the SMART system's coverage to air route traffic control centers in Atlanta along with Jacksonville and Miami in Florida, according to The Dallas Morning News. The FAA also shared an example with The Dallas Morning News about how SMART recommended a shorter and faster route for a cargo flight arriving at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, although the newspaper noted that the agency did not identify the flight involved and has not provided information about how SMART may have assisted passenger flight traffic.

The Dawn of the Data Intelligence Engineer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
09:08:18 UTC
18:08:18 KST

I asked Nick Ursa, our lead data engineer (and MotherDuck co-founder), how AI had changed his job. His answer: "This is the first time in my career with no backlog."
You'd think that would leave him with plenty of time on his hands, but he's busier than ever. While the backlog is gone, the answers still have to be right, and a human still has to decide how much quality control to do. Whereas once upon a time his job was to make sure the numbers he was computing were right, now his job is to make sure that the numbers that an LLM or agent comes up with are right.
That's a different job from working a ticket queue. At Data Outpost on November 4, I proposed a name for this new role: the Data Intelligence Engineer. I think it's now the emergent role on an AI-enabled data team, and I’d like to share why.
What a data team is for?
A data team has one job: enable the business to make good decisions. The faster they can make those decisions, based on a more accurate picture of what is happening, the better those decisions can be.
The hard part has been the route a question takes to become an answer. It moves like a relay. A marketing leader comes into work on Monday and notices that there was a spike in churn over the last week. Why did that happen? They file a ticket with the data team to investigate. An analyst picks up the ticket, and as they dig in, they realize some key data is not exported from one of the data sources. They file a ticket to ask a data engineer to look into it. That needs a change in one of the data pipelines, so the data engineer makes the change, tests it, runs the backfill, tests the backfill, and resolves the ticket. Then the ball is back in the court of the analyst, who can build the dashboard that was needed. By the time it ships, the marketing person can no longer remember why they asked in the first place. The churn rate recovered a couple of weeks later on its own.
This isn’t calling anyone out as not operating effectively or urgently; nobody in that relay did anything wrong. But every handoff means waiting, context is lost, and the half-life of the ability to effectively act on the answer to the question slowly decays.
As an aside, we should note that there was a whole generation of AI enabled tools that didn’t really help; the co-pilot era made some of the turnarounds faster, but the problem was that there were too many handoffs to be able to act quickly enough.
Something is different this time
Before December 2025, the case against AI for analytics was easy to make. LLMs wrote bad SQL. Business logic was unknowable. The sensible conclusion was that this was never going to work. In fact, I used to talk about how data teams were more or less exempt from the disruption that was happening in other areas of software.
Then, all of a sudden, the ground moved. New models got better at SQL. Business logic turned out to be something an agent can figure out with some helpful context. And agents went multi-turn, which means they don't have to get it right the first time. They can try a query, look at what came back, and try again, just like a human analyst would do. Put those together and it … just … works.
Self-service BI has been right around the corner for decades, what makes this different? Well, as a bit of an existence proof, here’s an example; the presentation I gave at Data Outpost was not created as a powerpoint deck or Google Slides, it was an app that I built using MotherDuck and Claude. I used live datasets from four different data sources, built a number of interactive and animated visualizations. Anything I did could be done by virtually anyone; I didn’t look at a single line of code or SQL.
It is important to stress that this isn’t just a way to automate building your dashboards. BI is typically pretty static, with maybe a couple of drill-downs. But with AI, you can build much richer visualizations. And what’s more, if you can build a dashboard with a prompt, you can go beyond that and also build a full-blown app.
Allowing business stakeholders to answer questions with data on their own has an even broader benefit than just shortening the data team’s backlog; it actually allows them to make better decisions. By cutting down the amount of time it takes and the number of handoffs involved, they can ask more questions. They can ask follow up questions while they still have all of the context in their heads. This means they can make confident decisions faster.
Which of these jobs can be a prompt?
AI is dramatically changing the job information workers perform. Software engineers often find their time being spent babysitting Claude sessions and rubber stamping agent-written code. What about the traditional roles of the data team? Which of their jobs, to put it a bit provocatively, can be a prompt?
As uncomfortable as the answer might be, rather a lot can be done via a prompt. In the not too distant future, writing SQL queries, creating dashboards, and building dbt pipelines are not going to be things that require specialized knowledge to do. Agents are likely better than humans at these tasks already, and they’re only going to get better. Our Data Engineer, Nick, moved us from one version of Airflow to another in a weekend, with minimal supervision, which once would have taken a week.
Writing code or SQL or building dashboards was never the whole job, though. The need for accurate data and the ability to understand it doesn’t go away. And someone has to be accountable, who can sign off and say “yes, this is right”. That takes a human in the loop. Quoth Nick, one more time, “Data eng, regardless of tooling or who does it, is an accountability function."
What still needs a human
Once agents are writing the code, what’s left in the data world? It turns out quite a lot. Humans need to make sure that other stakeholders without the world “Data” in their title are able to solve problems with data. That means they need to ensure a clean data model with appropriate context and annotations, a clear ontology to ensure that terms and concepts are being applied consistently throughout, and also they need to make sure that things continue to work.
These aren’t things that a model can intuit from data or history.  A model knows SQL. It doesn't know how your company counts revenue, or which of several similar-looking tables is the real one (it is revenue_cpx_new_revised_v2_use_this_one ) . A model doesn’t know that when the sales team talks about revenue they mean commissionable revenue, and the finance team uses something different.
Context is a crutch that is difficult to maintain. What’s even better is just building a clean data model in the first place. There is a good analogy with software; I tend to consider it a user experience failure any time any time your user has to read the manual; a cleaner design would have made whatever they were trying to do obvious. Context is just a manual for agents; if you can make the data model simple and clear enough, it can save them a lot of time and energy (and tokens).
Meet the Data Intelligence Engineer
The jobs to be done for a data person in the age of AI don’t really match any of the typical responsibilities of other data team members. I think it is different enough to merit a new title, which I hereby dub the “Data Intelligence Engineer”
The Data Intelligence Engineer automates the data engineer's work (ingestion) and the analytics engineer's work (transformation and modeling) by creating and conducting software agents. They encode their knowledge of the system into shared context that can be used by other agents to answer questions about the organization. These include things like which fields are joinable but also what someone in the company means when they say “ARR”.
Evals are another big part of their responsibility; these are the system tests that validate that when you ask questions with a known answer, the answer is correct. A good eval suite can give confidence that the types of questions that users ask of the system are going to be answered correctly by the agent. Evals also are a way of knowing when something breaks.
The goal of a Data Intelligence Engineer is to enable self-service. That is, anyone in the organization should be able to open Claude or ChatGPT or another agent and answer questions correctly about the business, use that to build apps and visualizations, and in the end, make high quality decisions with the benefit of data. . When the Data Intelligence Engineer does the job well, everyone who asks a question gets the experience of working with the smartest analyst in the company.
Day to day, that means they are going to be building frameworks, building the data model, curating the context, preventing things from getting broken, fixing them when they break anyway, running evals, and being accountable for the surfaces the business depends on. We wrote the whole thing up as a job description, because we believe this is the way things are going and it's time to give it a name.
If you're a data engineer, an analytics engineer, or an analyst, you'll recognize parts of this. Those roles were already blending into each other, and morphing into something new. This is a role you play, whatever your title says.
Won't this be chaos?
It's a fair question. More people building means more chances to be wrong, with less oversight. There is the possibility of making stupendously silly mistakes by acting on the wrong data. I’ll leave it up to the reader whether they think that stupendously silly mistakes are something new or not. The scary thing is that now the data team can be held responsible for them.
There are two things that help. The first is that the closer you are to the problem, the better you can spot errors. The person who lives with the churn number notices when it looks off. From experience, we’ve found that results actually improve because the business owner has a fingertip feel on their area; they know when something isn’t right, and can often spot problems even in the source data.
The other thing that helps is that you don’t need to watch everything with the same level of vigilance. Another quotable quote from our friend Nick is that “Agents need supervision proportional to their blast radius." That is, if something is going to be used for important reporting or decisions, you should pay a lot of attention. If you’re trying to figure out how many sandwiches to order for lunch, it probably isn’t going to cause a riot if you order too many with habanero mustard because Claude imagines it is extra tasty.
You can think of this in three circles of supervision. The outer is the Wild West. Anyone can build, they hopefully build on a reasonable foundation, but the data team keeps their hands off. The next tier is the Curated set. This is a set of dashboards, visualizations, apps, and metrics that is important to the business in some form or another. When something breaks in these dashboards, the data team should make a best effort to fix them. Finally there is the inner circle, the Core. This contains key metrics for the organization, things that are important to get right. The data team should make sure that these are high quality and predictable at all times. The board number lives in the Core.
What does this all have to do with MotherDuck?
On MotherDuck, we build mechanisms to empower your AI enabled data team. Flights are vibe-codable pipelines that can pull data into your warehouse and translate it into a sane model. Context lives in Guides, which are markdown files describing your data model and your business. A Guide starts out as private, but an admin can promote it to apply to the whole organization so that every person and agent works from the same definitions. We call the data visualizations that can be created by agents “Dives”. Every person and agent gets its own Duckling, a dedicated DuckDB instance. All of these are reachable from SQL, so one person or agent can work a problem across ingestion, transformation, context, and apps without a handoff between tools.
The only way out is through
We're in a chaotic moment. Chaos breeds the biggest opportunities, and the tools hand you some real super-powers if you're willing to pick them up. We're all learning how to do this together.
The data team isn't going anywhere. Someone still has to own the data model, curate the context, keep things working, and answer for the results. No-backlog-Nick has more to do than ever, and but the job is changing and not going back.
So who's doing this at your company, and what do you call them?
PS - if you want to see my slides from the talk, check out the Dive Gallery

The Netherlands Is Dismantling the International Criminal Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
07:55:49 UTC
16:55:49 KST

The Netherlands is negotiating with the US over the erosion of the powers of the International Criminal Court (ICC). This erosion is so drastic that, according to legal experts, it would amount to the dismantling of the Court. The Rights Forum has learnt this from diplomatic sources in New York, speaking on condition of anonymity.
The restrictions that would be under discussion include: a) granting immunity to heads of state; b) excluding the Court’s jurisdiction over nationals of non-state parties, even when they commit crimes on the territory of a state party; and c) denying the Court’s jurisdiction over cases covered by national legislation.
First and second restrictions
The first restriction would mean that heads of state and heads of government such as Netanyahu, Trump and Putin could not be prosecuted for crimes committed on their orders.
The second restriction would mean that the ICC could no longer prosecute nationals of non-state parties, even if they commit international crimes on the territory of a state that is a party to the Rome Statute – the founding treaty of the ICC.
Israel, for example, is not a party to the Rome Statute, whereas Palestine is. Consequently, under the current rules, the ICC can prosecute Israeli citizens and government officials for crimes they commit on Palestinian territory. On this basis, the Court has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant.
However, if the second restriction were to be adopted, Israeli nationals could no longer be prosecuted for crimes committed on Palestinian territory. The same would apply to US or Russian nationals who commit crimes on the territory of other States Parties.
This would undermine a key principle of the International Criminal Court: that nationals of states which have not ratified the Rome Statute can also be held accountable for international crimes.
Third restriction
The third restriction would mean that the ICC would no longer be permitted to hear cases if a state has legislation enabling it, in principle, to punish offences committed within its own jurisdiction. At present, the Court may still intervene if a state is unwilling or unable to investigate and prosecute suspects (the so-called principle of complementarity). If the third restriction were introduced, the mere existence of national legislation could be sufficient to prevent prosecution by the ICC.
For example: Israel has legislation against torture. It could therefore argue that the ICC has no jurisdiction, even if, in practice, cases of torture are not investigated or prosecuted. In this way, Israel could avert prosecution by the ICC without taking action against the perpetrators itself.
In short: if the aforementioned restrictions are adopted, there will be nothing left of the Court.
In order to enshrine these legal restrictions, the Rome Statute – which established the International Criminal Court in 1998 and under which it has operated since 2002 – would need to be amended. This would require a two-thirds majority of the States Parties. The amendment must then be ratified by seven-eighths of the States Parties before it can enter into force. It is not known which countries would cooperate in this regard.
US sanctions
The reason the Netherlands is said to be negotiating on this matter are the sanctions imposed by the US against thirteen judges and prosecutors, and against the ICC as a whole. This was done primarily in retaliation for the Court’s investigation into Israeli crimes in Palestine, and the resulting arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant. The undermining of the International Criminal Court by the US and Israel has now been going on for almost twelve years.
The Court has been on the US sanctions list since 9 October. However, a number of sanctions will not come into force until 7 April 2027. These would largely paralyse the institution, leaving the European Union with virtually no choice but to activate the far-reaching blocking mechanism. This law obliges European parties to disregard US sanctions and to continue supplying services and goods to the Court and its staff.
The EU, and EU countries like the Netherlands, are, however, reluctant to activate the mechanism due to the consequences it could have for European businesses. For instance, European banks that disregard the US sanctions might find it much more difficult to do business in the US – or could face sanctions themselves.
Opting for a compromise
That is why the Netherlands now appears to be opting for a compromise. By relinquishing certain aspects of the International Criminal Court, the US might be persuaded to lift or ease the sanctions against the Court. In practice, this would amount to amputating the Court’s limbs. What would then remain is a powerless trunk-court.
We are not quite there yet. The States Parties to the Rome Statute will meet in The Hague from 30 November to 7 December. The meeting was originally scheduled to take place in New York, but the US sanctions made it necessary to relocate it.
      
      Response from the ministry of Foreign Affairs    
    
    
      The Rights Forum has asked the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for a response to the reports, but it provides a general, meaningless statement and does not address the specific questions asked:
‘At the previous Meeting of States Parties (in December 2025), it was decided by consensus to encourage States Parties to engage in further dialogue with non-States Parties. In the run-up to the forthcoming Meeting of States Parties to the Rome Statute (30 November – 7 December), States Parties are continuing discussions on this matter and we are exploring the scope for dialogue with non-States Parties, within the framework of international law and with due regard for the independence and impartiality of the Court.
‘We cannot yet anticipate how such a dialogue will unfold, as this is not solely up to us: the Netherlands, together with the other 124 States Parties and our European partners, bears a shared responsibility to protect the Court. No concrete proposals are currently before the Assembly of States Parties.
‘In any case, we remain firmly committed to the Court and will continue to do our utmost to ensure it functions effectively: both as the host country and as a State Party. Independent courts and tribunals must be able to carry out their mandates unhindered. In these capacities, we also remain fully committed – together with other States Parties – to mitigating the impact of existing sanctions. It is important that the Court is able to function as freely as possible.’

Euclid Mission Data Release Spans More Than 900 Million Galaxies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Euclid Mission Data Release Spans More Than 900 Million Galaxies (reuters.com) 11
			
		 	
				The European Space Agency has released the largest dataset yet from its Euclid space telescope, containing 1.7 petabytes of observations covering more than 900 million galaxies. "The data unveiled on Thursday covered a survey of the sky equal to about 9,500 times the size of the moon as viewed from Earth," reports Reuters. "The mission's goal is to complete the "largest-ever three-dimensional atlas of the cosmos, spanning more than a third of the sky, in 2031." From the report:  "It marks a major milestone for ESA's Euclid mission and for everyone involved," said astrophysicist Valeria Pettorino, ESA's Euclid project scientist. Euclid, launched from Florida in 2023, is gathering data on how the universe has expanded and how its structure has formed over time while amassing information about the nature of dark energy and dark matter and the role of gravity on large scales.
"Euclid will not just take images of galaxies in the sky, in two dimensions, but will also measure their distance, the third dimension. This will tell us where galaxies are in space and time, across 10 billion years, and in all directions beyond our galactic plane," Pettorino said. "Galaxies cluster along filaments, surrounded by empty space, and form a network that we call the cosmic web. Euclid will reconstruct the cosmic web and how it has grown over time. This is important because the exact configuration of the cosmic web, how many clusters or voids are there, how fast it changed, depend on the properties of dark energy and dark matter," Pettorino said.
[...] Previous Euclid data releases covered only a few days of observations. The newly released dataset includes more than a year of data and still spans only 14% of the total sky area Euclid is due to survey in visible and near-infrared light over six years. This data release will be completed next year with the first results on dark energy and dark matter.

Global Microsoft Outage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
06:18:23 UTC
15:18:23 KST

Where things stand
• Hourslong outage: A Microsoft outage that began over 12 hours ago has left millions around the world without access to Outlook email, Teams meeting tools and other staples of modern office life. Banks, governments and courts in multiple countries are affected.
• No quick fix: The tech giant is struggling to fix the problem, which it said was not caused by a cybersecurity breach.
• Global disruption: Outage reports “reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour,” according to Downdetector. In the US, the House of Representatives said its engineers were working with Microsoft, and city governments nationwide reported widespread email disruptions. In the UK, a disruption to the National Health Service email system is expected to prevent some patients from getting their drug prescriptions.
Updates
(21)
Microsoft says services are being "gradually restored"
Microsoft says it is making “additional progress toward recovery” and that traffic is “being gradually restored” as its engineers scramble to fix the worldwide outage that has left millions without the work tools they use every day.
In a statement, Microsoft said it is “seeing improvements in key scenarios, including mailbox access and delayed email processing, though some intermittent issues may continue.”
What to know as you're waking up in the US without email
Outlook is still down, as Microsoft’s rolling outage – now extending into a second day – continues to affect services for millions of people around the world.
The outage, which is also affecting Teams and Copilot, is disrupting government and business operations in the United States and elsewhere, with at least one company postponing a quarterly earnings call.
Microsoft executivesCharles Lamanna said in the early hours of Friday that there is currently no indication that the outage is the result “of malicious or cyber activity.”
Here’s what to know:
Email down: Outlook remains down and users are also having trouble accessing their Exchange Online mailboxes.
In an update at around 4:15 a.m. ET Friday, Microsoft said it would extend its “email timeout window” to 48 hours “to help protect delayed messages while service recovery continues.”
The email timeout window is the maximum amount of time that a mail server or email client such as Outlook will spend waiting to receive an email before returning an error.
US lawmakers: The US House of Representatives said the outage impacted its users and its engineers were working with Microsoft, according to Reuters. Some congressional staffers expressed frustration on X. “Shall we start conducting all official business via DM?” said Sharon Eliza Nichols, communications director for Congresswoman Eleanor Holmes Norton.
US cities: City governments across the United States have reported email disruptions and have encouraged residents to call local offices and agencies if necessary.
- Several police and sheriff departments said the outage was affecting their email and communication platforms, including Colorado’s Arapahoe Sheriff’s Office, which said the outage had delayed the processing of prisoners’ bail payments.
- The outages are affecting email services in Miami Beach, Austin, and Jacksonville, though officials assured residents that emergency services were still active.
- In California, officials from Pasadena, Fremont, Burbank, and Santa Barbara also issued statements warning of downed email use.
- Baltimore County officials said on X that government staff could not send or receive emails and urged residents to contact relevant departments by phone.
Earnings call delayed: Workhorse Group, a Detroit-based electric vehicle manufacturer, pushed its third quarter earnings call to Monday, citing “business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outages.”
CNN’s Gage Goulding contributed reporting.
What is affected by the outage?
Some office workers rely on Microsoft’s suite of applications for practically everything – emails, meetings, AI, creating spreadsheets, and writing and sharing documents. Any of those functions which involve email or Microsoft’s Exchange Online services are impacted, the company said.
Outlook: Email is the main thing impacted by the outage, leaving users likely unable to access or send any new emails.
Copilot: Users may also be unable to load chats with or receive responses from Microsoft’s AI tool. Copilot also cannot access the data it normally draws from, like emails, files and calendars.
Teams: Anything that has already been scheduled and requires Teams — Microsoft’s communications platform — to connect with a user’s calendar is likely impacted. But if users are simply just joining a call or exchanging messages, that is still working.
Word/Excel/Powerpoint: The basic functions of these apps are still working. However, other functions may be impacted, like if users are trying to print documents over the cloud or share documents with Sharepoint. Users may also not be able to view their most recently used files.
Other, more specialist Microsoft services – like those which pool a company’s data or allow IT to monitor a company’s devices – may also be affected.
It's a disappointing day for some workers using Gmail
While many workers using Microsoft’s systems have spent Friday rejoicing that they’re forced to take a break — unable to send or receive emails or conduct their usual Teams calls — those using Google services are lamenting in memes shared on social media.
Google systems including Gmail, Google Docs and Google Meet appear to be functioning just fine, or at least well enough to promise users an average working Friday.
One video on Instagram shows someone lying in bed with the word “Outlook” above their head. Another sits at a desk working on their laptop with the word “Gmail” above theirs.
Another video shows a meme of actor Pedro Pascal appearing to sob uncontrollably under text reading: “When you hear Outlook is down and start planning your afternoon wines… Then remember your workplace uses Google Workspace.”
Railways report communications delay due to Microsoft service disruption
Some railway networks are experiencing disruptions to their customer email services and routing schedules because of the Microsoft outage.
VIA Rail Canada said passengers “may not be able to receive email communications about their trip” due to technical issues with Microsoft services. The railway asked passengers to check their web-based train tracker or subscribe to SMS notifications for information on their journeys.
Germany’s Deutsche Bahn said Microsoft Outlook is experiencing “severe sluggishness,” causing significant delays in its abilities to send out and receive emails.
“As a result, the distribution of rerouting schedules is severely restricted. All relevant teams are involved in resolving the issue; current indications point to a server-side problem on Microsoft’s end,” it said in a statement.
In the UK, National Rail, which runs passenger rail services in England, Scotland and Wales, said the ongoing outage may be affecting customers’ ability to access train tickets by email.
It advised travelers to visit the website or app where tickets were purchased, or to contact the ticket retailer directly.
“If you are still unable to access your ticket, please contact a member of onboard staff or station staff for advice,” National Rail said on its website.
Rail Delivery Group, which manages National Rail, said there were no current disruptions to operations or train services as a result of the outage.
CNN’s Nina Avramova contributed to this report.
Microsoft extends email timeout window to 48 hours amid outage
Microsoft said that it would extend its email timeout window to 48 hours “to help protect delayed messages while service recovery continues,” according to an update posted at around 4:15 a.m. ET Friday.
The email timeout window is the maximum amount of time that a mail server or email client such as Outlook will spend waiting to receive an email before returning an error.
Microsoft said recovery efforts are ongoing and that it’s seeing “early signs of stabilization,” though service capacity has not returned to normal.
It's Friday and Microsoft is still down. (Some) workers are taking it easy
Memes and jokes abounded online as the global outage of Microsoft’s Outlook emails and Teams meeting platform crossed the 12-hour mark.
One joke that spread on Threads, X and LinkedIn was the rebrand of Microsoft365 to Microsoft364 – memorializing the one day of the year that the software company went dark.
Others reveled at not needing to respond to constant emails and notifications for at least one day.
Another account wrote: “Outlook is down. Your email does not find me well. It does not find me at all.”
Others on Reddit said they panicked and thought they were laid off when they could not access their work emails.
Here's where we're seeing the outage's impacts
At first, Microsoft said the connection issues were happening “in the Americas,” but over time it became clear the troubles were global.
Microsoft’s outage reports “reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour,” according to Downdetector, a website that tracks cyber outages.
Here’s where we’ve seen reports of outages:
- Australian schools, courts and government services started their Friday morning with Microsoft Outlook and other apps out of service.
- In Hong Kong, workers from banks including Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs told CNN their work was disrupted, as they were unable to access emails or Teams from the moment they signed on and all through their lunch break. “Sporadically some mails come in but there is probably millions of backlog to process,” one banker told CNN before heading off for lunch break.
- The disruption has also hit Japan’s government services, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said in a Friday presser. Government employees are responding to the outage by creating physical copies of documents, he added. Government ministries and agencies have been unable to send emails through most of the Friday workday.
- Courts in the Philippines are also being slowed down by the Microsoft disruption, the Supreme Court said. “During this period, responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed,” it added in a post on X.
- In the UK, a disruption to the National Health Service email system is expected to prevent some patients from getting their drug prescriptions.
CNN’s Brian Stelter, Hilary Whiteman and Junko Ogura contributed to this report.
Britons can expect delays in accessing prescribed medication today, says UK pharmacy group
A Microsoft outage causing disruptions to the email system of the UK’s National Health Service is expected to prevent some patients from getting their drug prescriptions Friday.
The outage “affects a pharmacy’s ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients,” a spokesperson for the National Pharmacy Association said in a Friday statement.
GPs are equivalent to family doctors in the US.
An NPA spokesperson told CNN in a separate phone call that, while many patients will get their medications, those with more complex prescriptions requiring a pharmacist to contact the prescribing doctor to check or query any details could experience delays.
The spokesperson added that Fridays are typically busy days at pharmacies.
“It’s just a massive pain. It will be slow today,” they said.
Microsoft reports "marginal success" in patching servers
More than 12 hours after Microsoft first warned of a global outage affecting some of its most popular products, the company said it had “observed marginal success” in fixing the problem.
“We’re continuing to monitor activity across regions to evaluate server status and determine actions that can be taken to improve capacity,” Microsoft said in a statement posted on its Service Health Status page early Friday.
“At this point, we have observed marginal success,” the company wrote.
Around 30 minutes later, Microsoft posted another statement saying the company has seen “positive results for service stability and increased capacity as a result of our latest traffic optimization actions.”
Reiterating what it said earlier Thursday, Microsoft stated it was not aware of any malicious activity causing the outage but will continue to treat the incident “with urgency and priority until full resolution.”
More than 12 hours into Microsoft's outage, here's what to know
The Microsoft global outage is ongoing after the US tech giant first reported problems with its email services on Thursday.
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps and more than 90% of Fortune 500 companies use its Copilot AI chatbot, according to the company’s website.
Millions worldwide lost access to Outlook email, Teams meeting tools and other essentials of modern office life as the disruption quickly spread.
The company reported “marginal success” in repairing the outage in its latest update, early Friday ET. A Microsoft executive confirmed the outage was not the result of a security breach.
As Europe woke on Friday, the outage remained widespread.
Here’s the latest if you’re just tuning in:
- Return to sender: The outage hit in 74 countries and territories in around an hour, according to tracking website Downdetector. Several airlines reported disruptions to their email support.
- In the US: City governments countrywide reported widespread email disruptions and encouraged residents to call local offices and agencies if necessary. At least one American company postponed its quarterly earnings call.
- In Asia Pacific: Some of Japan’s government services switched to paper documents due to the outage and courts in the Philippines experienced delays. Australian schools, courts and government services were also affected. In Hong Kong, staff at Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs told CNN their work was disrupted through to their lunch break.
- Scams warning: Banks warned customers to beware of scams and phishing attempts as cybercriminals may use the outage to target individuals and businesses.
CNN’s Helen Regan, Hilary Whiteman, Karina Tsui, Kathleen Magramo and Ross Adkin contributed reporting.
Some airlines report comms disruptions due to Microsoft outage
Several airlines are reporting disruptions to their email support and communications due to the Microsoft outage, posting statements to customers on social media.
Indian budget carrier IndiGo said its “email support services are currently impacted, and we may not be able to receive your emails.” It directed customers to reach out via their website or mobile app.
Akasa Air, another low-cost Indian carrier, similarly said its “email support services are currently experiencing delays.”
And South African carrier CemAir said it was “experiencing some system disruptions due to the global Microsoft outage.”
None of the carriers reported flight disruptions.
Indian flag carrier Air India said it was “closely monitoring the ongoing Microsoft outage” and has rerouted emails. The airline said its flight operations “remain unaffected” and “there is currently no impact on any of our communication channels.”
“Consider this your cue to plan that getaway.”
Outage comes as Europe seeks to reduce reliance on US tech
The Microsoft outage comes at a time when Europe is pushing for greater tech sovereignty, aiming to run its own servers and reduce dependency on foreign providers.
Europe lacks the kind of mega tech companies that abound in the US, making it reliant on American firms for its digital services, but there is sentiment in Europe that it should become less reliant on the United States for its tech needs.
That sentiment has hardened during US President Donald Trump’s second term, when he has hit the continent with huge tariffs and threatened to take over the Danish territory of Greenland.
Earlier this year French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said that government officials will ditch Zoom and other US-owned video conferencing tools and begin using French-owned software. The decision is intended partly to reduce “dependencies on non-European actors,” Lecornu said.
“The internet in Europe is essentially a US construct, a US system. And Europe doesn’t really have a competitor to any of that,” Neil Shearing, group chief economist at Capital Economics, told CNN earlier this year.
On Friday, that question resurfaced as Microsoft’s outage stretched beyond 12 hours, disrupting countries across the globe.
“That tech sovereignty conversation, while it’s been mostly political, I bet it’s real sharp today,” technology journalist and founder of The Rip Current podcast Jacob Ward told CNN.
CNN’s Anna Cooban contributed reporting.
US cities report disruptions to email services
City governments across the United States have reported widespread email disruptions since Microsoft’s global outage began and have encouraged residents to call local offices and agencies if necessary.
The outages are affecting inbound and outbound email services at local government offices across major cities, including Miami Beach, Austin, and Jacksonville, though officials assured residents that emergency services were still active.
Baltimore County officials said on X that government staff could not send or receive emails and urged residents to contact relevant departments by phone.
In California, officials from the cities of Pasadena, Fremont, Burbank, and Santa Barbara also issued statements warning of downed email use.
Several police and sheriff departments said the outage was affecting their email and communication platforms, including Colorado’s Arapahoe Sheriff’s Office, which said the outage had delayed bond payments for prisoners.
Scammers may take advantage of Microsoft outage, banks warn
Banks and financial institutions are warning customers to beware of scams and phishing attempts as cybercriminals may take advantage of the global Microsoft outage to target individuals and businesses.
“Stay alert and protect yourself,” Standard Chartered Singapore said on social media. “A technology outage can create opportunities for scammers.”
The Bank of Queensland said that scammers may ask for personal details or One-Time Passwords and warned customers to “hang up immediately” if they receive a suspicious call.
Customers have been advised to not click on links or open attachments from unknown sources, and never share PINs or passwords. Other banks have told their customers to be cautious of anyone claiming to be tech support personnel, and to report unauthorized transactions and suspicious messages.
Technology journalist Jacob Ward told CNN that the “the ripple effects” from the outage could “go on and on.”
Laura Sharman contributed reporting.
Outage forces US electric vehicle maker to postpone earnings call
The Microsoft outage has caused at least one American company to postpone its quarterly earnings call.
Workhorse Group, a Detroit-based electric vehicle manufacturer, pushed their Q3 earnings call to Monday, citing the technology outage.
Earnings calls are typically held virtually, either via a conference call or video webcast system, allowing company executives to discuss financial results with investors and analysts. Participants dial in by phone or join online.
Workhorse postponed its earnings call until Monday, November 16 at 4:30 p.m. ET.
Global outage not caused by cyber attack, Microsoft executive says
The global Microsoft outage was not caused by a cybersecurity breach, a Microsoft executive confirmed late Thursday.
“We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity,” Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, said in a post on X.
Earlier, Australia’s Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the company had told him that they “don’t believe they are dealing with a cyber attack.”
“They believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke added during a press conference in Sydney.
Burke was referring to the 2024 software glitch at cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike that crashed computers, canceled flights and disrupted hospitals all around the globe, causing billions of dollars in losses.
Australia’s spy agency and federal police were among the organizations hit by the Microsoft outage on Friday local time.
Outage shows global risks of companies relying on a handful of tech giants, experts say
The Microsoft outage highlights the “inherent dangers” of companies that depend on a handful of tech giants for critical global infrastructure, an expert told CNN.
“If one of those firms suffers a major outage, it has the potential to dramatically reduce business productivity globally during the outage time,” Computing Professor Toby Murray, of Australia’s University of Melbourne, said.
Murray added that the outage affecting Outlook and other major services like Microsoft Teams is “incredibly widespread, and its ramifications extend well beyond being able to send and receive work emails,” making it difficult for businesses to operate.
Mark Gregory, Associate Professor at Australia’s RMIT University School of Engineering, also said the outage highlights how dependent businesses and government agencies have become on technology providers.
it was “unthinkable” that a company like Microsoft could have a global outage after previous incidents.
Gregory was referring to the 2024 software glitch at cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike that crashed computers, canceled flights and disrupted hospitals all around the globe, causing billions of dollars in losses.
He highlighted the need for better contingency plans when critical services go offline.
Microsoft says still no "sustained recovery"
Microsoft said it had not yet observed a “sustained recovery” in areas affected by the widespread outage.
“We’re continuing our efforts to improve server stability to improve traffic flow,” it said late on Thursday in a post to its X account for Microsoft365 service incidents.
“We’re observing partial recovery across regions in which we’ve applied these adjustments; however, these actions aren’t resulting in sustained recovery.”
Outage causes headaches for some and jokes for others
Some US office workers celebrated the email blackout and joked that they could start the weekend early.
Others barely missed a beat, connecting with colleagues via Slack, phone and even the old-fashioned in-person way.
But the outage, which began around noon on the US East Coast, caused serious headaches, especially when it dragged on for more than an hour or two.
In Australia, Friday began with a realization that the Microsoft cloud was unresponsive. The outage took out live feeds from courts, and schools texted parents to phone in any absences until email systems were restored.
Australia’s national broadcaster, ABC, reported people missing job interviews because they couldn’t connect to virtual meetings, and even some supply issues with distribution centers stocking supermarkets due to the outage.

Customers have been advised to not click on links or open attachments from unknown sources, and never share PINs or passwords. Other banks have told their customers to be cautious of anyone claiming to be tech support personnel, and to report unauthorized transactions and suspicious messages.
Technology journalist Jacob Ward told CNN that the “the ripple effects” from the outage could “go on and on.”
Laura Sharman contributed reporting.
Outage forces US electric vehicle maker to postpone earnings call
The Microsoft outage has caused at least one American company to postpone its quarterly earnings call.
Workhorse Group, a Detroit-based electric vehicle manufacturer, pushed their Q3 earnings call to Monday, citing the technology outage.
Earnings calls are typically held virtually, either via a conference call or video webcast system, allowing company executives to discuss financial results with investors and analysts. Participants dial in by phone or join online.
Workhorse postponed its earnings call until Monday, November 16 at 4:30 p.m. ET.
Global outage not caused by cyber attack, Microsoft executive says
The global Microsoft outage was not caused by a cybersecurity breach, a Microsoft executive confirmed late Thursday.
“We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity,” Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, said in a post on X.
Earlier, Australia’s Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the company had told him that they “don’t believe they are dealing with a cyber attack.”
“They believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke added during a press conference in Sydney.
Burke was referring to the 2024 software glitch at cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike that crashed computers, canceled flights and disrupted hospitals all around the globe, causing billions of dollars in losses.
Australia’s spy agency and federal police were among the organizations hit by the Microsoft outage on Friday local time.
Outage shows global risks of companies relying on a handful of tech giants, experts say
The Microsoft outage highlights the “inherent dangers” of companies that depend on a handful of tech giants for critical global infrastructure, an expert told CNN.
“If one of those firms suffers a major outage, it has the potential to dramatically reduce business productivity globally during the outage time,” Computing Professor Toby Murray, of Australia’s University of Melbourne, said.
Murray added that the outage affecting Outlook and other major services like Microsoft Teams is “incredibly widespread, and its ramifications extend well beyond being able to send and receive work emails,” making it difficult for businesses to operate.
Mark Gregory, Associate Professor at Australia’s RMIT University School of Engineering, also said the outage highlights how dependent businesses and government agencies have become on technology providers.
it was “unthinkable” that a company like Microsoft could have a global outage after previous incidents.
Gregory was referring to the 2024 software glitch at cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike that crashed computers, canceled flights and disrupted hospitals all around the globe, causing billions of dollars in losses.
He highlighted the need for better contingency plans when critical services go offline.
Microsoft says still no "sustained recovery"
Microsoft said it had not yet observed a “sustained recovery” in areas affected by the widespread outage.
“We’re continuing our efforts to improve server stability to improve traffic flow,” it said late on Thursday in a post to its X account for Microsoft365 service incidents.
“We’re observing partial recovery across regions in which we’ve applied these adjustments; however, these actions aren’t resulting in sustained recovery.”
Outage causes headaches for some and jokes for others
Some US office workers celebrated the email blackout and joked that they could start the weekend early.
Others barely missed a beat, connecting with colleagues via Slack, phone and even the old-fashioned in-person way.
But the outage, which began around noon on the US East Coast, caused serious headaches, especially when it dragged on for more than an hour or two.
In Australia, Friday began with a realization that the Microsoft cloud was unresponsive. The outage took out live feeds from courts, and schools texted parents to phone in any absences until email systems were restored.
Australia’s national broadcaster, ABC, reported people missing job interviews because they couldn’t connect to virtual meetings, and even some supply issues with distribution centers stocking supermarkets due to the outage.

Company reliance on one system makes outages like this a severe challengepublished at 10:17 GMT
10:17 GMT
Jaltson Akkanath Chummar Asia business producer
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Single tech outage can impact multiple business functions
Today’s disruption of Microsoft services highlights the risks faced by businesses that rely heavily on a single technology provider for major operation needs.
Companies generally go for one particular tech company like Microsoft or Google for their email, meeting and software needs as it's easier to manage a single provider and is more cost effective.
But that makes tech outages a more severe challenge for those businesses.
"When several critical services depend on the same provider, one disruption can affect multiple business functions simultaneously. This is known as concentration risk," says Bernard Tan from global technology firm Protiviti.
He says the issue isn't relying on one major provider, but whether "companies understand these dependencies and have practical alternatives when services become unavailable," Bernard told the BBC.
"A more practical approach is to invest in alternative arrangements for the services that are most important to their operations," he added.

Scientists claim the universe is twice as old as believed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
05:13:30 UTC
14:13:30 KST

The universe could be 26.7 billion years old, almost twice as old as scientists generally believe, according to a researcher at the University of Ottawa (uOttawa) who says his model also works without dark matter or dark energy.
Rajendra Gupta, an adjunct professor of physics, and postdoctoral researcher Nikolaos Samaras have spent much of the past two years checking their model, known as CCC+TL (Covarying Coupling Constants plus Tired Light), against major astronomical observations.
Instead of relying on undetected dark matter and dark energy to explain the cosmos, CCC+TL modifies the laws of gravity and cosmic expansion by proposing that physical constants slowly shift over time and that light loses energy as it travels across space, meaning distant light took far longer to reach us, extending the universe’s estimated age to 26.7 billion years per the model.
“Most emerging models explain only a limited set of observations,” Gupta said in a statement. “A new model must not conflict with the pillars of cosmology and astrophysics, and our findings meet that challenge, including the yet-to-be-published Cosmic Microwave Background challenge.”
Putting the theory to the test
In computer simulations testing the framework, the researchers found that their model accurately predicted the observed abundance of hydrogen and helium created in the Big Bang, while also matching the universe’s historical expansion rate without requiring dark energy.
In a study published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the team reported that their model could also explain how stars and gas orbit in 175 galaxies, something that has long been one of the main arguments for dark matter.
The model could also help with a puzzle raised by the James Webb Space Telescope, which has found galaxies that seem far too big and developed for how early in the universe’s history they appear. If the universe is older, those galaxies would simply have had more time to grow.
“The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously,” Gupta noted. “It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the Universe beyond ΛCDM limits.”
The idea is still well outside the mainstream. Some of the team’s work is still under review, and the standard model continues to explain a wide range of observations, so other scientists will need to test the findings independently. Upcoming Webb observations that search for even more distant galaxies could help.
Sources: uOttawa, Monthly Notices, MDPI, Science Daily

The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
05:10:27 UTC
14:10:27 KST

The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
The average transaction cost for a new vehicle has reached a record high: $51,109. That's according to a report out today from the Kelley Blue Book, which is part of the analytics firm Cox Automotive.
That's about $500 above the last record, set in December 2025.
Car prices have been stubbornly high for years, especially since the pandemic, mainly driven by supply chain issues. And they've gotten higher recently, in part thanks to tariffs and to buyers flocking to, and car companies making, larger, fancier vehicles.
Yet there's a little good news: Cars are getting more expensive … more slowly.
While that $51,109 figure is an all-time high, that's only up 2.1% in the past year.
"A 2.1% year-over-year increase is actually below inflation," said Erin Keating, an executive analyst at Cox Automotive who co-authored the report. Between 2012 and 2021, cars got 3.4% more expensive a year on average, she continued.
The Kelley Blue Book's transaction cost is based on what people wound up paying for a new vehicle — that means whatever's on the sticker price, plus add-ons for fancier features, and minus any incentives, such as dealer discounts.
It also doesn't include one other expense that adds to the cost of owning a car: interest on auto loans. The cost of borrowing has risen over the past several years as the Federal Reserve has kept interest rates high in an effort to drive down inflation. Auto loan rates are now about 11% for used vehicles and over 7% for new ones, according to Edmunds, a car analytics company.
Keating says all of this can add up to some sticker shock for buyers — partly because people don't buy cars all that often and can be surprised by how expensive they've gotten, and partly because of interest rates.
"I mean, we are seeing a true shift in the percentage of your monthly payment that's going towards interest versus towards principal," she said.
Used cars are not a steal
The Kelley Blue Book's average includes all kinds of vehicles — SUVs, pickup trucks, electric vehicles — from all kinds of auto companies, including Toyota, Subaru, Tesla and Mercedes-Benz.
It doesn't, however, include used car sales, which normally make up about two-thirds of total sales. Ivan Drury, director of industry insights at Edmunds, crunched those numbers too and found the same trend. "No matter what you're looking at, the price is up," he said.
The average used car now costs close to $27,000, 6% higher than last year, according to Cox Automotive. Vehicles that cost less than that are a "sliver" of the industry, Drury said.
Supply chain challenges, including a semiconductor shortage, during the COVID pandemic meant fewer cars got made. Carmakers had to pick and choose which vehicles to prioritize making — they picked their most profitable models. As a result, fewer used vehicles entered car lots in the early 2020s. So today there's less inventory to choose from.
That's good for people who already own a car, Drury said. It means people can upgrade to a new car without much additional money up front.
But, he continued, "The consumer that I sympathize with the absolute most? The first-time car buyer." Those buyers face a steep down payment, with nothing to trade in.
No matter whether buyers are choosing new or used, data from Edmunds shows that in 2026, they have been financing with lower down payments and longer auto term lengths. "We've just seen those explode," Drury said.
A report from Edmunds found that car buyers financed more than ever, taking out loans worth an average of $44,664 in the past quarter. They also found that more than a quarter of car buyers financed using loans with 84-month-long terms — or longer.
The combination of a small down payment — sometimes in the range of $500 or $1,000 — and a lengthy loan term can get really expensive for buyers in the long term, Drury said, especially with high interest rates.
"So people just say, 'Oh, forget it,' you know. 'I'll just, I'll just choose the longer term length and put less money down. I've got other bills that are pulling at me,'" Drury said.
Why are new cars so expensive?
In part, vehicles cost more because the cost of making them has gone up for automakers. There are now more tariffs on steel and aluminum, as well as on goods imported from Canada. That matters for American automakers who assemble vehicles on both sides of the border. The cost of computer chips (used in sensors and electronics) and copper (used for automotive wiring) has also risen thanks to competing demand from data centers.
But vehicles also cost more because Americans like bigger cars, SUVs and trucks, which tend to come with a higher price tag. The average sticker price for a full-size pickup truck is nearly $72,000, according to the Kelley Blue Book.
American carmakers have largely shifted their gears away from compact sedans. In earnings calls with investors, they've often cited American demand for bigger vehicles.
Plus, as analyst Mike Wall at Mobility Global points out, smaller vehicles offer lower margins for carmakers. "They were sort of that loss leader. It gets the eyeballs in the door," he said.
For the carmakers, they're not making as much money as they would compared to their bigger vehicles with pricier features.
Drury notes, people appreciate those features. They've gotten used to driving with 360-degree cameras, heated seats and parking assist systems. All of these drive up the cost of buying. "No one wants entry-level anymore," he said. "Everybody goes mid-to-upper trim levels."
"People love walking up to their car that already has the air conditioner going when it's 110 degrees outside, and think, 'You know what? I don't have to get in here and potentially burn my hands,'" Drury continued. "So as we get accustomed to more features, more options, we naturally kind of pile on, too. And automakers, they're very aware of that."
A challenging time for automakers
Over the past few years, "automakers have been under incredible stress," Keating said. Yes, there are tariffs and other rising production costs. Many also poured money into developing electric vehicle technology, but EVs still only make up a small slice of the U.S. car market. About 6% of new cars sold are electric, according to Edmunds.
And the market for car buyers is smaller. About 16 million people buy new cars every year — about 1 million fewer since the pandemic.
Notably, fewer people in their late 30s and early 40s are buying cars. "They're just simply holding onto their cars longer," Keating said. Her hypothesis? "That age group and that cohort is simply just dealing with different household pressures for their money and are making the choice to stay in the vehicles that they have."
For the most part, the people buying new cars tend to be older and wealthier. Keating said that might be because older drivers are staying on the road longer. " We have seen this interesting shift towards individuals keeping their licenses longer and therefore more 65 and up, 75 and up individuals are purchasing vehicles than ever before," she said.
For automakers, a drop in car buyers means they have to compete more with each other for sales.
"At the end of the day, each of these competitors are sharing, trying to go after a pie that isn't necessarily growing," Keating said. So instead, " they're stealing share from their competitors as opposed to counting on more consumers entering the picture."

Show HN: PharmA2A, an open protocol for pharmacy-to-supplier orders on A2A
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
04:58:53 UTC
13:58:53 KST

The open protocol for direct orders between a pharmacy and its suppliers, labs, wholesalers and buying platforms, on top of A2A.
Version 0.1, published on 12 November 2026. Site: pharma2a.org. Contact: contact@pharma2a.org. Version française.
In France, a community pharmacy orders directly from hundreds of suppliers: dermocosmetics, supplements, medical devices. Every order is a form, a mail, a phone call, then a check at delivery. PharmA2A fixes what the pharmacy's buying agent and the supplier's agent say to each other, so that an order is right the first time and the supplier learns, when the pharmacist allows it, what its products do on the shelf.
A2A (Agent2Agent, Linux Foundation) says how two agents talk.
PharmA2A says what they say: five messages, each a JSON Schema, declared as an A2A profile
extension, https://pharma2a.org/ext/v1. To our knowledge,
it is the first sector-specific dictionary built on A2A.
The field names are French: PharmA2A starts with French community pharmacy, its CIP 13 codes and its words. The specification and the English guide explain every message in English.
- No economic data of the pharmacy in any message. The supplier's own terms travel as it states them, never recomputed.
- Nothing invented. A field nobody stated stays null.
- Only the supplier speaks for the supplier, and a transcribed answer never confirms an order on its own.
- A message that says nothing is not a confirmation.
- The pharmacy calls, the supplier answers. No push, no stream.
- No patient data.
An order is transmitted once: the reference is its identity, per customer account.
The pharma2a package also carries what every part uses: the dictionary and its validation (pharma2a.dictionnaire).
Python 3.11 or newer.
git clone https://github.com/pharma2a/pharma2a && cd pharma2a
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate && pip install -e ".[modele,test]"
The sample supplier, in one minute. Start it, then let the demo pharmacy order from it:
python examples/sample-supplier/agent.py
python -m pharma2a.officine --agent http://127.0.0.1:8766 --attendre 2    # in a second terminal
The supplier email bridge. It starts in draft mode: nothing is sent, mails are written to sorties/.
PHARMA2A_JETON=a-test-token python -m pharma2a
PHARMA2A_JETON=a-test-token python -m pharma2a.officine       # in a second terminal
Its agent card is at http://127.0.0.1:8765/.well-known/agent-card.json. Every setting is an
environment variable, listed in .env.example. python -m pytest runs the tests.
- Specification: the normative rules, for anyone who implements PharmA2A.
- The protocol in detail: the messages, the diagrams, the rules, A2A conformance.
- Connecting a supplier system: the backend contract, an ERP round trip in 10 minutes, the dictionary mapped to ERP fields.
- Decision records: why the protocol is the way it is.
- The guide: the complete guide for a supplier's IT staff, installation and configuration included. Version française.
- The dictionary itself: schema/, with an example of each message in schema/exemples/.
The pharmacy buying agent that SyderaAI (Paris) runs for its pharmacies speaks PharmA2A with their suppliers. No supplier runs an agent yet, so that buying agent hosts the supplier email bridge for each supplier: the supplier gets a clear mail with the order in its body, answers as usual, and the bridge transcribes the answer into the dictionary. The day a supplier serves its own agent, the pharmacy changes one URL.
Pharmacy buying agents that speak PharmA2A:
To add yours, open a pull request that adds one line to this table: the agent's name, its publisher, and a contact. Pour ajouter le vôtre, ouvrez une pull request qui ajoute une ligne à ce tableau.
Issues and pull requests are welcome: see CONTRIBUTING.md,
GOVERNANCE.md and CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md. Security
reports go through SECURITY.md, never through a public issue. Versions are in
CHANGELOG.md.
The dictionary (schema/) is public domain, CC0 1.0. The agent and its tests are Apache 2.0.
PharmA2A is a trademark of SyderaAI, Paris, filed with the French INPI: the content is free,
the name is not, see TRADEMARK.md. Anyone may implement, copy, fork and extend
the protocol without asking; the name is protected only so that nobody can call "PharmA2A" what
does not follow it, which is what keeps the common language common.

IceWM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
04:54:53 UTC
13:54:53 KST

IceWM is a window manager for the X Window System. The goal of IceWM is speed, simplicity, and not getting in the user’s way. It comes with a taskbar with pager, global and per-window keybindings and a dynamic menu system. Application windows can be managed by keyboard and mouse. Windows can be iconified to the taskbar, to the tray, to the desktop or be made hidden. They are controllable by a quick switch window (Alt+Tab) and in a window list. A handful of configurable focus models are menu-selectable. Setups with multiple monitors are supported by RandR and Xinerama. IceWM is very configurable, themeable and well documented. It includes an optional external background wallpaper manager with transparency support, a simple session manager and a system tray. IceWM is available on popular Linux distributions like Debian, Ubuntu, Arch, OpenSUSE, Gentoo, Slackware, CentOS, antiX, NixOS and on most *BSDs.
Software
IceWM was created by Marko Maček in 1997 using C++. It is now maintained at Github.
Releases
The latest released version is 4.1.0 (2026-08-06).
Features
- Easy to use, simple and fast
- Standards compliant→
- Fully usable with keyboard
- Alt+Tab window switching
- Efficient resource usage
- Task bar (optional)
- Multiple workspaces
- Fully documented→
- A large number of themes→
- Usable with GNOME and KDE environments
- Regenerates menus when configuration changes
- Support for sound effects→
- Multiple focus modes
- Manual placement of windows option
- Autoraising of windows option
- Tooltips
- Configurable keybindings→
- Supports DockApps in a container
- Tabbed windows
Screenshots
The IceWM Screenshots Collection
Themes
IceWM is themeable.
The visual appearance of icewm can be changed by a theme,
which is a collection of settings and small images.
Over 450 themes can be downloaded from box-look.org.
Extra is a collection of 91 highlights. See icewm -i list.
Translations
IceWM is translated into three dozen languages. To improve the translation for your language at Weblate, first register an account either here or there, then update.
Documentation
Bug Tracking
Report your icewm bugs on Github. Only report it once and give relevant details.
Install the latest release as follows
$ wget https://github.com/ice-wm/icewm/releases/download/4.1.0/icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz
$ tar -x --lzip -vpf icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz
$ cd icewm-4.1.0
$ ./configure --prefix=/usr
$ make
$ sudo make install
Install from unreleased development source code
Gettext must be installed.
$ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm
$ cd icewm
$ ./autogen.sh
$ ./configure --prefix=/usr
$ make
$ sudo make install
If you have cmake, an alternative is:
$ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm
$ cd icewm
$ ./rebuild.sh -r --prefix=/usr
$ cd build
$ sudo make install
Install package dependencies
To install all package dependencies in one go use the following script.
$ wget https://ice-wm.org/scripts/os-depends.sh
$ sudo bash -x ./os-depends.sh
Verify package dependencies by:
$ pkg-config --modversion x11 xext xcomposite xcursor xdamage xfixes xres xrender xrandr xinerama xft fontconfig sm ice sndfile alsa ao gio-2.0 gio-unix-2.0 gdk-pixbuf-xlib-2.0 imlib2 librsvg-2.0 xpm libpng libjpeg
# or simpler:
$ ./rebuild.sh -d
More installation and configuration

- Extended window manager hints.

- Alt+Tab window switching
- Efficient resource usage
- Task bar (optional)
- Multiple workspaces
- Fully documented→
- A large number of themes→
- Usable with GNOME and KDE environments
- Regenerates menus when configuration changes
- Support for sound effects→
- Multiple focus modes
- Manual placement of windows option
- Autoraising of windows option
- Tooltips
- Configurable keybindings→
- Supports DockApps in a container
- Tabbed windows
Screenshots
The IceWM Screenshots Collection
Themes
IceWM is themeable.
The visual appearance of icewm can be changed by a theme,
which is a collection of settings and small images.
Over 450 themes can be downloaded from box-look.org.
Extra is a collection of 91 highlights. See icewm -i list.
Translations
IceWM is translated into three dozen languages. To improve the translation for your language at Weblate, first register an account either here or there, then update.
Documentation
Bug Tracking
Report your icewm bugs on Github. Only report it once and give relevant details.
Install the latest release as follows
$ wget https://github.com/ice-wm/icewm/releases/download/4.1.0/icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz
$ tar -x --lzip -vpf icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz
$ cd icewm-4.1.0
$ ./configure --prefix=/usr
$ make
$ sudo make install
Install from unreleased development source code
Gettext must be installed.
$ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm
$ cd icewm
$ ./autogen.sh
$ ./configure --prefix=/usr
$ make
$ sudo make install
If you have cmake, an alternative is:
$ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm
$ cd icewm
$ ./rebuild.sh -r --prefix=/usr
$ cd build
$ sudo make install
Install package dependencies
To install all package dependencies in one go use the following script.
$ wget https://ice-wm.org/scripts/os-depends.sh
$ sudo bash -x ./os-depends.sh
Verify package dependencies by:
$ pkg-config --modversion x11 xext xcomposite xcursor xdamage xfixes xres xrender xrandr xinerama xft fontconfig sm ice sndfile alsa ao gio-2.0 gio-unix-2.0 gdk-pixbuf-xlib-2.0 imlib2 librsvg-2.0 xpm libpng libjpeg
# or simpler:
$ ./rebuild.sh -d

SpaceX To Invest $74 Billion Into Data Center Construction Projects In Texas, Arizona

SpaceX To Invest $74 Billion Into Data Center Construction Projects In Texas, Arizona 19
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from the Hill: Elon Musk's SpaceX plans to invest more than $74 billion into building two data centers in Texas and Arizona, the company announced Thursday, marketing them as projects that will boost local communities amid backlash surrounding such facilities. "These investments will expand local tax bases, generate substantial new revenue for schools and public services, and create economic opportunities that extend far beyond the facilities themselves," the company said in a release. SpaceX said it will put more than $24 billion into a new project in Texas's Rio Grande Valley, expanding the company's headquarters in Starbase -- a coastal town the tech giant established in 2025 in a previously unincorporated area of Cameron County. In Arizona, SpaceX will invest around $50 billion in Cochise County, a rural area east of Tucson bordering Mexico and New Mexico.
SpaceX pledged the new projects will be created cooperatively with the surrounding communities and will be environmentally conscious. The company said the project in Texas would generate its own power and invest $220 million to expand the water supply in nearby Brownsville. While in Arizona, it vowed to work with local electric cooperatives and "potentially" reduce electric bills, saying the site would use dry cooling without water consumption. "They require strong partnerships with local communities, responsible environmental stewardship, and stable, competitive policies that give companies the confidence to make long-term investments," the company said in a release. Both sites promise hundreds of permanent jobs even once construction is complete.
