No, AI agents did not discover a previously unknown Maya site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-12
19:42:40 UTC
04:42:40 KST

Armed with a team of AI agents, Google researcher Pietro Miotti claimed earlier this week to have discovered a potentially unmapped Maya site in Mexico. There was just one problem: The site had already been discovered and was published in an academic journal last year. The incident, which sparked criticism among archeologists online, underscores a growing tension in science as amateurs wielding increasingly powerful AI tools parachute into specialist fields, often without the expertise needed to understand what they are looking at.
No, AI agents did not discover a previously unknown Maya site
Scientists are getting tired of amateurs parachuting into their fields and making ‘discoveries’ with AI.
Local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area.
Miotti said the idea to use AI to search for archeological sites came to him while traveling in Peru, when he began wondering what historic explorers might do with access to modern technology. He settled on lidar, a laser-based mapping technology that can produce detailed three-dimensional images of the environment, and set a team of 48 AI agents to comb through NASA lidar data for signs of undocumented sites. As “Peru isn’t well covered” by public lidar data, Miotti wrote, he shifted his focus to the Maya region.
The agents flagged numerous promising locations, including “one major village [that] doesn’t seem to have been registered” in existing records. Miotti, who described the research to The Verge as a personal side project done without any Google compute or resources, said he then reached out to Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) to check whether the apparent discovery was already known, including through unpublished research. Using the agents to translate his correspondence into Spanish, Miotti said INAH told him it had no record of a registered site at that location.
“It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive,” Miotti wrote on his blog.
Miotti stressed that he is not an archeologist and emphasized that the finding would need to be verified with fieldwork. Nevertheless, he hailed it as proof that “we’re on the brink of a revolution across every science” and called for the “entire planet” to be mapped with lidar so AI agents could “help us find the rest.” Had he been an archaeologist familiar with the region, however, Miotti might have spotted a problem: The site was already known, and had been documented in an academic journal more than a year earlier.
“I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.”
Archeologists were quick to point out the oversight on social media. In a series of posts on Bluesky, Sarah Parcak, an archeology professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, stressed the importance of carefully checking findings against existing research. “This is why we have peer review,” Parcak wrote, adding that just because the Mexican government doesn’t have something in its database doesn’t mean it is unknown or unmapped. Other archeologists echoed her criticism, slamming the project for spreading misinformation and taking credit away from archeologists, who have been using advanced digital tools in their work for decades.
“This was a personal project that I was excited to share,” Miotti told The Verge. “I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.” He added that as a non-archaeologist, he had not realized a site not being registered wasn’t the same as it not having been mapped, adding that expert knowledge “is needed to verify what the agents find.” He also addressed the limits of his AI tools: “My agents and I missed it. Archaeologists rightly don’t publish the coordinates of sites, so checking whether a site is already known means comparing images against figures in papers, not searching a database. That’s much harder for agents, and it’s something these tools need to get better at. When people pointed it out, I updated the post and the blog as soon as I could to credit their work.”
Nevertheless, Miotti said this was an example of how agents could be used to help experts sort through large amounts of data. He said he has been encouraged by the archaeologists and PhD students that he said were reaching out to him “excited about the workflow and wanting to know how it works and whether it could help with their own survey data.”
“Our ‘problem’ is not discovering new sites,” Elizabeth Graham, a professor of Mesoamerican archaeology at University College London, told The Verge. “Most of us working in the Maya area know about tons of sites not explored or excavated or mapped, most of these found on foot,” she said. Graham also critiqued the use of the word “discover,” noting that local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area.
While she credited Miotti with doing a decent job of using AI to map the mounds from lidar data — “the interpretation of lidar data can be tricky” — Graham argued the bigger obstacle is funding for research. “The fact is, there just isn’t the funding to excavate or map sites as there was in the past, so in a way it doesn’t matter how many more are ‘discovered.’”
“Just spotting something does not add much to our knowledge.”
The controversy reflects a broader problem with AI in science, perhaps most visible with OpenAI’s recent advances in mathematics. While AI tools are increasingly capable of producing genuinely impressive results, they don’t always engage with the existing research those findings build upon. The result can be claimed breakthroughs that have, as is the case here, already been made by someone else, or a general failure to credit earlier work. Even when the findings are actually new, they can lack context a specialist would bring. Ultimately, amateur use of AI tools often ends up shifting the burden of establishing what has actually been found and why it matters to actual experts, work that would ordinarily be part of making a scientific discovery in the first place.
Ivan Šprajc, a professor of archaeology at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts in Ljubljana and a coauthor of the paper documenting the site, told The Verge he wasn’t particularly impressed by the agents’ work. Archeologists have been using lidar and “other sophisticated remote sensing tools for quite some time,” he said, adding that “just spotting something does not add much to our knowledge.” He told The Verge that while it is commendable that Miotti checked in with INAH, doing so is “not sufficient” as the institution does not have access to all possible information. “The fact that INAH has no official knowledge of a particular cluster of archaeological features does not necessarily mean that it has not been spotted or even explored by archaeologists.”
Šprajc said that he worries the growing use of AI tools by amateurs could overwhelm archeologists with claims of new discoveries. “Just today I have received an email from another AI ‘discoverer,’ so I am a little bit concerned about being flooded by this kind of message,” he said. He also raised another potential risk of amateurs publicizing the locations of archeological sites: attracting looters. “But as long as these findings do not lead to looting, I don’t see a major problem,” he added.

Google’s latest Search upgrade promises better answers to your most complicated questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-12
19:27:45 UTC
04:27:45 KST

Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos. The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.”
While Google’s frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, are best at deep reasoning for hard problems, Hydrogen is designed for fast execution across a variety of agentic workflows, or tasks in which an AI carries out multiple steps on its own, the company explained in an announcement.
The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do. Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, its previous fast model, but it’s still pretty smart, even beating the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on one broad intelligence benchmark, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, at its default high thinking level.
In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode.
In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly. This means people can ask their questions in their natural train of thought, including those that have multiple parts or that include highly specific requests. Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says. Because of its improvements and better ability to follow instructions and call the right tools, Hydrogen is able to more precisely address each part of a user’s question.
Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries. This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains.
The addition of Hydrogen to Search will also mean more images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools will appear as visual responses to users’ queries in AI Mode.
Google also says Hydrogen can work on its own for everyday work in areas like writing code, running tests, or verifying code changes, or it can be paired with Carbon and Argon in workflows that combine several models.
The model offers four thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and a new, extra-high tier (“xhigh”), all of which are designed to complete tasks faster with fewer output tokens.
On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks No. 5 on Agent Arena’s benchmarks, the company pointed out.
In addition to Search, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is coming to all tiers of Google’s AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google’s Antigravity development platform.
Google says the Hydrogen update is rolling out to all Search users globally.

How We Tested Chef’s Knives Under $35
- The tomato test. To start, I ran each knife through an heirloom tomato to produce two or three thin slices. I was looking to see if the knives squished the tomato, left some of the skin behind, and/or could achieve a paper-thin slice.
- The sweet potato test. To up the ante, I then used each knife to slice and dice a sweet potato. Sweet potatoes can be hard to cut through, as they are quite starchy on the inside. I was looking to see how much, if any, resistance each knife met while cutting the sweet potato, if the blades got stuck at any point while slicing, and if the blade could slice straight down through it.
- The hand-washing test. At the end of all this slicing and dicing, I put the knives through one more test: hand-washing. Hand-washing is the recommended way to clean knives, so I used lukewarm water, dish soap, and a soft sponge on each blade. I was looking to see how easy it was to scrub the blades clean and if there was any staining left behind.
Why You Should Trust Me as a Tester
I’ve been reviewing the best products for your home, kitchen, and beyond since 2022. In that time, I’ve tested hundreds of kitchen products alone, including cookware, knives, small appliances, meal delivery services, and lots of condiments. I only write about the ones that truly impress me and I’d be willing to pay for with my own money. Someone once told me that a negative review doesn’t help anyone, but a positive review actually tells someone where to go, what to eat, or what to buy. And that’s become my professional MO.
What Makes the Best Budget Chef’s Knife
- Sharp 8-inch blade. What’s a knife without a sharp blade? This is, in my humble opinion, the most important feature of any knife. For a chef’s knife, the blade is often 8 inches. Although other lengths are available, I find 8-inch knives offer the most versatility while also being easy to store.
- Comfortable to hold. Whether you’re quickly slicing up an apple or spending some time chopping up produce, meats, and cheeses for your weekly meal prep, having a knife that feels good in your hand makes such a difference. I find ones with rounded handles feel the best; even better if it has a rubber-like grip.
- Easy to clean. No one wants to spend time relentlessly scrubbing away over the sink. A knife that has an easy-to-hand-wash blade and handle is a must, and it shouldn’t have staining from the food you were cutting left behind after it’s washed.
- Sheath for safe storage. It’s not unusual that budget knives come with a sheath. This is a feature I actually wish my higher-end knives came with because it makes them way easier to store. Plus, some budget knives come with self-sharpening sheaths that can help maintain the blade.
Other Knives We Tested
- Sabatier Forged Stainless Steel Chef’s Knife. This $19 knife is outfitted with a self-sharpening sheath, like the Farberware knife, which I love. But it had a hard time slicing through the sweet potato, and it left my thumb feeling strained, which is why it didn’t make the cut (no pun intended!)
- J.A. Henckels International Statement 8-Inch Chef’s Knife. This $27 knife did a great job thinly slicing the tomato, but it struggled with the sweet potato. This, coupled with the fact that it has a boxy handle that strained my pointer finger and wrist, kept it from beating out the top three knives.
Frequently Asked Questions
- How should I clean my knife? Hand-wash it, for sure. You might be tempted to toss it into the dishwasher (trust me, I am, too), but you’ll get more longevity out of the blade by hand-washing it. You’ll want to dry it completely right after, too, to keep the blade in tip-top shape.
- Can I sharpen my knife at home? Absolutely! You can use a honing steel if you have one (some knife blocks include them), or you can pick up a rolling sharpener, like The Original Tumbler. It’s a little bit of a splurge, but it doesn’t take long to get the hang of and can be used on other knives you have, too.
- Can I store my knife in a drawer? If it has a sheath, totally. Otherwise, I wouldn’t recommend it, just because it’s easy for the knife to get caught while opening the drawer (which could damage your knife) and it’s easy to get accidentally nicked this way. If you have some space in a knife block, try storing it there. If you have absolutely nowhere else to store it but a drawer, I would recommend wrapping the blade in a thick kitchen towel in an effort to protect the blade and your hands.

Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-12
19:11:00 UTC
04:11:00 KST

Nectar, an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.
Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.
Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically.
Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN. The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult.
Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords.
Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular.
Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets.
“Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.”
Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a new baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals.
Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers.
The company plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents.
This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic.

Vibes Don't Maintain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-12
19:06:29 UTC
04:06:29 KST

Vibes Don't Maintain
Since ChatGPT took off, people have been coming up to me to say some version of “you people will be out of a job soon.”
Most of them were managers. They knew it was provocative, and they wanted to see how I’d react - partly to test the waters on whether this was a real scenario. What they had in common was that none of them had a clear idea of what software development actually is. Not what it looks like from the outside. What it is.
Last week I got the best version of that conversation I’ve had so far.
A friend of mine owns a restaurant. He told me he’d built an app for it with Claude Code - a web app to manage tasks and processes for his staff. He was proud of it, and he had every right to be. He had never written a line of code and he had a thing on a screen that did what he described.
I had a look. It was nice. Clean layout, sensible flow, data that persisted between page loads so it felt like a working system.
Then I started poking. No responsive layout - it broke on the phones his staff would actually use. No dark mode 🏴☠️. No login, so no notion of who did what. No settings. No translations, in a kitchen where half the team doesn’t speak the language the app was written in. No error states. No handling of the empty case, the duplicate case, the two-people-edit-the-same-thing case. The data “persisted” in a way that would survive a refresh and not much else.
It was a click-dummy. A prototype. A perfectly good proof of concept for a first round of conversations about whether the idea holds up - which is a real and valuable thing to have.
Then he asked me if I could host it for him and do ops.
This is the biggest misunderstanding people have about software, and it has nothing to do with AI.
People see the surface. They see the parts that work. They don’t see the parts that run when something goes wrong, the parts that exist to stop things going wrong, or the parts that have never once executed in production because they’re there for a worst case someone sat down and imagined.
The seatbelt and the airbag in your car have, with luck, never done anything. That doesn’t make them useless. You don’t buckle up because the law says so or because the car beeps at you. You buckle up because you understand that one day you might need it. Software is mostly seatbelts. The happy path - the thing the demo shows - is the smallest part of the codebase.
My friend, understandably, didn’t see that. His read was that the app works 100% as intended, so 90% of the work is done. The rest is hosting. And I shouldn’t overcomplicate it.
Here’s how that version plays out.
The prototype came almost free and almost instantly. He decides the product is done. He might even get it in front of users - his staff start using it for real shifts, real tasks, real schedules.
Then something goes wrong. The database file corrupts. A dependency update breaks something. Someone finds the app on the open internet and has a look around. An edge case fires that nobody wrote down. Or my personal favorite: daylight saving time, and every shift in the schedule is off by an hour.
Everything goes boom.
He doesn’t know what he built. He doesn’t know why it was built the way it was - the reasoning lived in a chat session that’s gone. He doesn’t know what to look for or where to start looking. There is no spec, no test, no document, no commit message that explains the intent of anything.
At that point he has two options. Find someone to fix it and prepare to hand them all his money, because the first week of that engagement is pure archaeology. Or flee the country.
That is what “vibes don’t maintain” means in practice. The vibe got him to the demo. Nothing carried forward from there.
None of this is “don’t use AI.” We use it every day. But two things are true at the same time.
First: AI does not make you a software engineer if your background is baking bread, any more than your oven at home makes you a chef. It makes execution cheap. It does nothing about knowing what to execute, or what to do when the execution fails.
Second: shit in, shit out. If the input is a loose description of what the happy path looks like, the output is a happy path. The AI will not invent the seatbelts for you. It doesn’t know you’ll need them, because you didn’t.
What survives a boom is not the code. It’s the record of what the code was supposed to do - the stories, the specs, the decisions - written down somewhere a human or an agent can read them back. Ours are markdown files in git, kept with bacon-tracker. My friend has a chat history he can’t find anymore.
That record is what you’re paying for. Not the click-dummy.
There’s a second question hiding in his request, and in all those “you’ll be out of a job” conversations: if the tool really can do my job, what exactly was I still for? But that’s for another day.
I called him the next day. I told him I got myself a Thermomix - the one with AI - and was planning to open a restaurant the week after.
He laughed. Then he went quiet for a second.
I hope he got it. But knowing him I think he did not.

Dwarf planet candidate appears which takes roughly 280 years to orbit our sun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-12
19:05:33 UTC
04:05:33 KST

Astronomers Found a Mysterious Object Orbiting Far Beyond Pluto. It Could Be a New Dwarf Planet Hidden in Our Solar System
The dwarf planet candidate, called ED138, appeared in telescope images and takes roughly 280 years to orbit the sun. Astronomers need to determine its size to properly classify it
Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, was sifting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile when something odd caught his eye. Running a custom-made computer program, he and his colleague Kevin Napier had already spotted more than 2,000 little bright dots in the telescope data, corresponding to newly discovered small objects in the distant solar system. But this one was different: It seemed to be big.
Holman managed his expectations. After all, astronomers in the business of finding distant objects are used to disappointment. “We all have ‘found Mars’ … in terms of a false positive,” Holman tells Smithsonian magazine. They find a bright object that seems really big, then, with a closer look, learn that it’s nothing very remarkable after all. “We’re all really cautious when you see something that looks like it’s large.”
Still, this object grabbed Holman’s attention, so he tried to verify it with Napier and Rubin solar system lead scientist Mario Jurić. They found the celestial body in previous photos of the sky throughout the past decade, which helped them zero in on its orbital path—and the more historical data they found, the more confident they became.
“We know that it’s real,” Holman says. “Every time you look at the predicted location, there it is.” They even found it in photographic plates from 1937, stored in the Harvard plate stacks, he says.
The object, called 2026 ED138, is 46 times farther from the sun than Earth is, and it takes 281.1 years to complete an orbit. Now, the central question is whether it’s big enough to be classified as a new dwarf planet, which would put it among the rare ranks of only five other objects in our solar system.
“This is incredibly exciting,” Paul Byrne, a planetary scientist at the Washington University in St. Louis who was not involved in the discovery, tells National Geographic’s Robin George Andrews. “It heralds a new era of solar system and planetary science.”
Dwarf planets are smaller planets that orbit a star and have a nearly round shape, which happens naturally with objects above a certain size, as their gravitational force pulls evenly on all sides. But dwarf planets are not large enough for their gravity to clear their orbital paths of similar-size debris—the eight planets of our solar system, meanwhile, have achieved that feat. (Pluto’s designation was changed from planet to dwarf planet in 2006 for this reason—its orbit is littered with icy Kuiper Belt objects.)
Quick fact: Dynamic dwarf planet
Ceres, a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, may contain salty water that can percolate onto the surface in some regions.
ED138 is likely big enough to be round and, therefore, a dwarf planet—estimates for its size currently range from 370 miles to 930 miles across. But astronomers will have to confirm that measurement, and from the object’s brightness alone, that’s impossible. A highly reflective, smaller object, perhaps covered in gleaming ice caps, might appear just as bright as a less reflective, duller body that’s much larger.
Astronomers have two ways to get the required data. They could observe the world in infrared light, which reveals the thermal energy that it emits after being warmed by the sun. “From that you can figure out how big it is, because we know approximately what temperature it should have,” Holman says.
Alternatively, astronomers could watch the dwarf planet candidate pass in front of a star. If they know how much light comes from that star and how fast ED138 is moving, they can calculate the body’s size based on how long it obscures the light.
Holman says people are working on making those observations with telescopes such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). The dwarf planet candidate isn’t extremely easy to see at the moment, he adds, but “in the next few months it will be, and people will try.”
Right now, astronomers recognize five dwarf planets: Pluto, Eris, Makemake and Haumea in the distant Kuiper Belt, and Ceres in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Experts have long suspected that there could be more of these objects, but many of them could have highly elliptical orbits that keep them too far away for us to see most of the time. What we observe is potentially the “tip of the iceberg of a few that are in the close part of their orbit,” Holman says. “There must be a lot that we just haven’t yet detected.”
The discovery also hints at a relatively unexplored area of our solar system—the region that’s in front of the dense, starry core of the Milky Way from our perspective. It’s harder to pick out objects against all the background light in that zone, and ED138 has been traveling through it for the past 25 to 30 years, Holman notes. “There’s a swath on the sky where we really don’t have a good idea of what is there,” he adds.
What’s more, ED138 is in the southern hemisphere’s sky, and a lot of astronomical observations have focused on the northern hemisphere. But Rubin is poised to help change that: The new telescope, which has the world’s largest digital camera and captured its first images last year, is one of several observatories operating out of Chile’s Atacama Desert.
“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth and precision,” Jurić says in a statement.
“I was surprised that it found such an object so early,” Megan Schwamb, a planetary scientist at Queen’s University Belfast in Northern Ireland and a member of the Rubin solar system operations team, tells CNN’s Jacopo Prisco. “This was not on my bingo card for this year.”
Understanding more about how and where ED138 formed could reveal new details about the early days of the solar system. And its existence offers a clear reminder that surprising objects remain to be found on the fringes of our planetary neighborhood.
“Is there a Mars- or Earth-size or bigger object out there?” Holman says. “That’s not ruled out.”

Microsoft said its Outlook email service is currently experiencing an outage, preventing both business and consumer users from accessing their inboxes.
The issue was initially flagged as affecting the U.S. and the Americas, and later expanded to affect “any region.”
Microsoft hasn’t given a specific cause, but said that it was providing updates in its admin center, which wasn’t reachable at the time of publication. Microsoft says its video conferencing tool Teams, file sharing platform SharePoint, and its AI tool Copilot are also unavailable. The company says its Defender XDR security system is also affected by the outage.
Consumers are also unable to access their OneDrive storage, Office (for the web), and several other Microsoft services during the ongoing outage.
TechCrunch will reach out to Microsoft for comment, as soon as our own email service has resumed.
The company’s last major incident was in September, when a days-long outage hit Microsoft 365, its online productivity suite that includes Outlook. During that outage, Microsoft blamed a “core authentication configuration” issue that prevented users from accessing the service.

Google Pushes Privacy Angle As Gemini-Powered Smartglasses Debut
Unknown

Google Pushes Privacy Angle As Gemini-Powered Smartglasses Debut (arstechnica.com) 24
			
		 	
				Google is launching its first Gemini-powered smart glasses, with Samsung supplying the computing hardware. Given their built-in 12-megapixel camera, Google is emphasizing privacy protections, including a tamper-resistant recording light, automatic face redaction, and restrictions on real-time facial recognition and livestreaming. The company also promises not to use captured photos or videos for AI training or targeted advertising. Ars Technica reports:  Google says the frames all weigh about 41 grams, which is not terrible but is definitely near the top for glasses generally. They will, naturally, weigh much more when you account for lenses. That will also determine the final pricing. So far, we only have the starting prices for these devices, including non-prescription lenses.
The setup here is similar to the Ray-Ban Meta glasses we've seen for a few years. There are no screens in the lenses, but you can interact with the AI system via voice or by activating the integrated camera. The experience should be similar to using Gemini Live on your phone, but it will be a lot easier to fire up the AI. You can say "Hey Gemini" or tap a touch-sensitive area of the frame to start interacting with the robot.
Since this is the same chatbot that operates across the Google ecosystem, it has access to your data and preferences. You can ask questions and get personalized answers, have Google Maps guide you by voice, or just talk with the AI to kill time. The glasses use custom open-ear speakers to limit distractions for those around you. Google notes the directional microphones should not pick up speech from other people, either.
Adding the camera feed is where things get interesting. When the AI can see what you see, it has the potential to do more work on your behalf. Google suggests asking Gemini for recommendations when looking at a bookshelf or glancing at an event poster to have the AI add it to your calendar. The glasses will also support Gemini Guided Vision, which provides conversational audio descriptions for people who are visually impaired.  The new frames are available for preorder today starting at $395.

Thanksgiving Delight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-12
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Thanksgiving Delight
This make-ahead treat has it all: graham cracker crust, pecan pie filling, whipped cream cheese, chocolate pudding, and fluffy whipped cream.
Serves9 to 12
Prep40 minutes
Cook5 minutes
Why You’ll Love Thanksgiving Delight
- Pecan pie meets chocolate pudding. The gooey pecan filling pairs perfectly with chocolate pudding, plus cream cheese to make it not-too-sweet.
- No oven required. The pecan filling cooks on the stovetop, leaving your oven free for the rest of Thanksgiving dinner.
- You can make it the day before. An overnight chill sets the layers for clean slices and takes dessert off your holiday to-do list.
I became a pecan-lover sitting under a tree. When I was growing up on a farm in Arkansas, we’d gather pecans by the bucketful every November. I’d sometimes take a break, back against the trunk of our enormous pecan tree (the biggest in the state, according to my dad), and squeeze two pecans in my hand until the shells cracked, sneaking a snack. Every year my grandma would turn some of this bounty into a pecan pie for Thanksgiving dinner. The nostalgic farm chore (along with Grandma’s delicious pie) is one of my favorite Thanksgiving memories now.
This Thanksgiving delight takes that love of pecan pie and transforms it into a stunning five-layer dessert. Here, gooey pecan pie filling joins cream cheese, chocolate pudding, and whipped topping over a buttery graham cracker crust. It’s entirely no-bake, so you won’t have to negotiate for oven space, and an overnight chill means dessert is ready before the turkey even goes in.
Straight from Our Recipe Tester
“What a delightful dessert! I loved all the layers, from the tangy cream cheese layer which cut through the sweet pecan pie layer to the chocolate layer that rounded everything out. It’s rich for sure, but not too sweet or heavy. I can’t wait to share this with loved ones during the holidays.” —Kristina, October 2026
Why You Should Trust Me
I’ve spent the 15 years since culinary school honing my skills across New York City kitchens, from restaurants and catering to high-volume test kitchens and food media, including Rachael Ray Every Day, Food Network, and an eight-year stint at HelloFresh. I’ve developed and tested hundreds of recipes over the years and pride myself on their reliability, ease of use, and flavor payoff. I caught the baking bug when I won a blue ribbon at the county fair for my maple leaf sugar cookies at age 8.
Key Ingredients in Thanksgiving Delight
- Graham crackers: Crushed graham crackers combine with melted butter to form the buttery, no-bake crust. Use whole sheets or store-bought crumbs.
- Pecans: Toasting brings out their rich, nutty flavor. Finely chopped pecans go into the filling, with more scattered on top for crunch.
- Dark corn syrup and brown sugar: Give the pecan pie filling its gooey texture and deep, molasses-rich sweetness.
- Cornstarch: Thickens the stovetop pecan filling (no eggs necessary!) so it holds its shape when chilled and sliced.
- Cream cheese: Adds tang to balance the sweet layers. Let it come to room temperature before beating for a smooth, fluffy filling.
- Instant chocolate pudding mix: Makes the chocolate layer easy to prepare. Be sure to use instant pudding, not cook-and-serve.
- Whipped topping: Lightens the cream cheese layer and finishes the dessert with a fluffy topping.
Helpful Swaps
- Try using an equal amount of candied pecans for the topping in place of plain.
- Swap the instant chocolate pudding for instant vanilla or pumpkin spice pudding.
Thanksgiving Delight Recipe
This make-ahead treat has it all: graham cracker crust, pecan pie filling, whipped cream cheese, chocolate pudding, and fluffy whipped cream.
Prep time 40 minutes
Cook time 5 minutes
Serves 9 to 12
Nutritional Info
Ingredients
For the crust:
- 8 tablespoons (1 stick) unsalted butter, melted and cooled
- 12 whole graham cracker sheets (6 1/2 ounces), or 1 1/2 cups graham cracker crumbs
- 1 tablespoon granulated sugar
- 1/4 teaspoon kosher salt
For the pecan layer:
- 1/2 cup whole milk
- 2 tablespoons cornstarch
- 1/2 cup dark corn syrup
- 1/3 cup packed dark brown sugar
- 1/4 teaspoon kosher salt
- 3 tablespoons unsalted butter
- 1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1 cup finely chopped toasted pecans
For the remaining layers:
- 8 ounces cream cheese, at room temperature
- 1 (8-ounce) container thawed whipped topping, such as Cool Whip, divided
- 1/4 cup powdered sugar
- 1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1 (3.9-ounce) box instant chocolate pudding mix
- 1 1/2 cups cold whole milk
- 1/2 cup finely chopped toasted pecans
Instructions
Make the crust:
- Line an 8x8-inch square baking pan (about 2 inches high) with 2 sheets of parchment paper, positioning them perpendicular to each other, so that the parchment hangs about 2 inches over all 4 sides of the pan to form a sling.
- Break 12 whole graham cracker sheets into rough pieces and place in a food processor. Add 1 tablespoon granulated sugar and 1/4 teaspoon kosher salt. Process until the crackers are the texture of sand, about 15 seconds. Add 1 stick melted and cooled unsalted butter and pulse to combine, 6 to 8 (1-second) pulses. (If using graham cracker crumbs, just stir 1 1/2 cups crumbs, the sugar, salt, and the butter together in a medium bowl.)
- Transfer to the baking pan. Use the bottom of a flat measuring cup or your fingers to press the crumbs into an even layer, making sure to reach the edges and fill the corners. Refrigerate while you make the pecan filling.
Make the pecan layer:
- Whisk 1/2 cup whole milk and 2 tablespoons cornstarch together in a small saucepan until smooth. Whisk in 1/2 cup dark corn syrup, 1/3 cup packed dark brown sugar, and 1/4 teaspoon kosher salt. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a flexible spatula and scraping the bottom and corners of the saucepan, until thickened and bubbling throughout, about 5 minutes.
- Turn off the heat. Stir in 3 tablespoons unsalted butter and 1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract until the butter is melted and incorporated. Stir in 1 cup finely chopped toasted pecans. Let cool, stirring occasionally, until no longer warm, about 30 minutes.
- Dollop evenly over the crust. Using an offset spatula, gently spread into an even layer. Refrigerate until cold and set, about 45 minutes.
Make the remaining layers:
- Beat 8 ounces room-temperature cream cheese, 1/4 cup powdered sugar, and 1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract together in a stand mixer with the paddle attachment on medium speed, scraping down the bowl once or twice, until very light and fluffy, about 3 minutes total.
- Fold in 1 cup of the thawed whipped topping by hand with the flexible spatula until combined. Dollop over the pecan filling and spread into an even layer. Refrigerate.
- Whisk 1 (3.9-ounce) package instant chocolate pudding mix and 1 1/2 cups cold whole milk together in the now-empty mixer bowl (no need to clean) until slightly thickened, 1 to 2 minutes. Let stand until thickened, about 5 minutes. Dollop over the cream cheese mixture and gently spread into an even layer.
- Dollop the remaining thawed frozen whipped topping (about 2 cups) over the pudding and spread into an even layer. Cover and refrigerate until set, at least 4 hours or up to overnight.
- Sprinkle with 1/2 cup finely chopped toasted pecans. Grasping the excess parchment, lift the slab out of the pan and place on a cutting board. Cut into 9 to 12 pieces, wiping the knife clean between each cut for the cleanest-looking slices.
Recipe Notes
Toasting pecans: Toast in a skillet over medium-low heat, stirring frequently, until fragrant, about 5 minutes. Let cool completely before chopping.
Substitutions
- You can use light corn syrup instead of dark corn syrup in the pecan pie filling. It will be lighter in color and have a slightly less robust flavor.
- 3 cups sweetened whipped cream can be used in place of the frozen whipped topping.
Storage: Refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container for up to 4 days.

The Saddest Stray You Ever Did See
Posted on November 12, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi 31 Comments
WARNING: THE FOLLOWING CAT PHOTOS MAY BE DISTRESSING TO SOME READERS (no gore, just.. a really rough looking cat.)
Another day in Bradford, another stray cat. Though, this time it isn’t a kitten, it’s a very, very rough looking guy that has reportedly been out on the streets for at least a year. I have never seen a cat in this sort of state before, it’s truly shocking how he’s even alive, honestly. Here’s who I am referring to as Big Grey:
The longer I looked at him and petted him, the more I saw wrong with him. So matted, so dirty, so in need of care and love. He broke my heart.
Worst of all, there is literally a rag that is just like, fused to him:
I know he looks rough, but he is extremely sweet and affectionate:
He is very gentle and timid, it was very surprising. Well, he was that way until I snatched him and put him in my garage. Now, he is not so happy with me. In fact, I was going to take him to the vet today, but he will not let me get close to him without hissing and swiping at me. I know he’s just scared, but I desperately need him to let me put him in a carrier and that is just not happening right now.
In the meantime, he’s been eating wet food and drinking water, and he’s used the litterbox I put out for him. I put out a blanket for him but every time I’ve checked on him he is pretty much petrified in the corner of the garage. I feel so bad I’m scaring him, but I’d like to think it’s for his own good in the long run.
Yesterday, before he was even caught, I called twenty, TWENTY shelters and rescues in the area and either got no answer with no voicemail set up, or got told they were either completely full already or just simply didn’t take cats at all. There’s one place that does TNR but their waitlist is a month or even two out, and I want more care for this cat than just TNR.
I know he’s sweet. I know he likes head scritches and pets. I know he doesn’t meow or yowl or make any noise, even when in the carrier. He goes in a litterbox, he eats (or ate, previously) Churu right from the tube in my hand. I know there’s a big, beautiful, fluffy grey cat under there that just needs love. He will be a good companion, I just know it.
Since I can’t get him to a vet currently, I am going to try to regain his trust and affection over the next few days by hanging out with him in the garage and feeding him, and I can only hope he’ll adjust soon.
I’ll keep y’all updated.
-AMS

Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-12
18:52:01 UTC
03:52:01 KST

Explore our next generation products
Built for developers and teams in the agent-first era
Everything you need to stay up-to-date and get help
Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator
Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with our strongest models for long-horizon tasks, including Gemini 4 Carbon, in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency.
Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator
Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside /swarm for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems.
For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves.
Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster.
- Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks.
- Fast, dependable execution with Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Hydrogen also works as a standalone model for everyday coding and agentic work, scoring 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (surpassing Argon’s 50, and reaching 54 at its highest setting) and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (more than tripiling 3.8 Flash’s 18.2%). When selecting Hydrogen directly, you can dial reasoning depth across four thinking levels, low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier.
Getting started
Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out as Orchestrator (Carbon) and Orchestrator (Argon) for Google AI Ultra subscribers, and as Orchestrator (Argon) for paid Google AI Pro subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business.

Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-12
18:39:23 UTC
03:39:23 KST

The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.
Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models.
Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community.
Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion. Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source, whatever happens next.
Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.
Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development.
Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.
Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.
Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China.
The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections.
That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons.
Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.
Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls.
Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed.
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers.
More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs.
Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment.
This article has been updated with information from an Nvidia employee.

Rust 1.100
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-12
18:39:05 UTC
03:39:05 KST

The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.
If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, you can get 1.100.0 with:
$ rustup update stable
If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0.
If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel (rustup default beta) or the nightly channel (rustup default nightly). Please report any bugs you might come across!
What's in 1.100.0 stable
Never type
After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable! This also completes the project goal for this work.
The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return, break, and std::process::exit, also have the type !.
Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn ! into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a match or an if:
fn mrrrow(option: Option<u32>) {
    let value = match option {
        // `x` has type `u32`
        Some(x) => x,
        // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`,
        // allowing the `match` to pass type checking.
        None => return,
    };
    // ...
}
While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions (-> !), this release allows naming the never type anywhere:
fn infallible_unwrap<T>(res: Result<T, !>) -> T {
    // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before
    let Ok(v) = res;
    v
}
Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using !. This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization).
Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible, we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024. This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable.
We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it.
Allocator API
This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api, enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box. These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait.
This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon!
DropGuard: run a closure on every exit path
The Drop trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we return, ?, or panic. Drop being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket.
Implementing Drop can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing core::mem::DropGuard: a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped.
DropGuard takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements Deref and DerefMut so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable.
DropGuard also implements a dismiss method which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure:
use std::mem::DropGuard;
use std::num::ParseIntError;
/// Attempt to parse all `strings` and push them into `nums`.
/// If parsing any of them fails, `nums` remains unchanged.
fn parse_all(nums: &mut Vec<u32>, strings: &[&str]) -> Result<(), ParseIntError> {
    let len = nums.len();
    let mut nums = DropGuard::new(nums, move |nums| {
        nums.truncate(len);    // ← 1. Reset the vec on failure
    });
    for s in strings {
        nums.push(s.parse()?); // ← 2. If `?` returns an error, roll back
    }
    DropGuard::dismiss(nums);  // ← 3. Parsing successful, dismiss the guard
    Ok(())
}
Conjuring zero-sized types
As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this.
This question is answered in Rust 1.100 with a single function: std::mem::conjure_zst.
Instead of transmuting (), MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init(), or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing.
Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's Python<'py> is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition.
Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo
Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds.
Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every bin in a package when only some may use it.
Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g.
warning: unused dependency `tracing-subscriber`
  --> Cargo.toml:23:1
   |
23 | tracing-subscriber.workspace = true
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default
help: consider removing the dependency on `tracing-subscriber`
A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table.
For example, running cargo check --bin foo won't show warnings for unused [dependencies] because another bin may be present that uses them.
No warning will be shown for unused dev-dependencies because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built.
This warning is being introduced as part of a new linting system for Cargo, controlled by the [lints.cargo] table in Cargo.toml, completing this project goal. See also the other lints that have been introduced.
Reducing Cargo cache collisions
Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the build-dir and then uplifts final artifacts to the target-dir. At this time, these share a common parent directory.
Different build configurations, like --features, can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the build-dir.
These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints.
This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on.
These problems get exacerbated when sharing a build-dir across git worktrees.
The build-dir now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory.
This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal, unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking.
We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases.
Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns
Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns.
You can opt in via .cargo/config.toml:
[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "3 days"
When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back:
$ cargo update
    Updating crates.io index
     Locking 2 packages to highest compatible version as of min-publish-age
      Adding cc v1.11.0 (available: v1.18.0, published 3 hours ago)
      Adding clap 4.6.7 (available: 4.6.9, published 2 days ago)
When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update:
$ CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE=allow cargo update clap --precise 4.6.9
    Updating crates.io index
    Updating clap 4.6.7 -> clap 4.6.9 (published 2 days ago, minimum age 3 days)
The newer version will be recorded in Cargo.lock and kept from then on until a later cargo update re-resolves it.
A few things to keep in mind:
- This depends on the registry recording when each version was published.
Versions without a pubtime field in the index are never held back.
- cargo install ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies.
Pin a version with cargo install foo@1.2.3 if needed.
- Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would.
Further work to protect the ecosystem is planned under the crates.io supply chain hardening project goal, including quarantine support and automated detection of suspicious releases.
Stabilized APIs
Other changes
Check out everything that changed in Rust, Cargo, and Clippy.
Contributors to 1.100.0
Many people came together to create Rust 1.100.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!

fn infallible_unwrap<T>(res: Result<T, !>) -> T {
    // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before
    let Ok(v) = res;
    v
}
Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using !. This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization).
Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible, we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024. This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable.
We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it.
Allocator API
This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api, enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box. These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait.
This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon!
DropGuard: run a closure on every exit path
The Drop trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we return, ?, or panic. Drop being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket.
Implementing Drop can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing core::mem::DropGuard: a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped.
DropGuard takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements Deref and DerefMut so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable.
DropGuard also implements a dismiss method which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure:
use std::mem::DropGuard;
use std::num::ParseIntError;
/// Attempt to parse all `strings` and push them into `nums`.
/// If parsing any of them fails, `nums` remains unchanged.
fn parse_all(nums: &mut Vec<u32>, strings: &[&str]) -> Result<(), ParseIntError> {
    let len = nums.len();
    let mut nums = DropGuard::new(nums, move |nums| {
        nums.truncate(len);    // ← 1. Reset the vec on failure
    });
    for s in strings {
        nums.push(s.parse()?); // ← 2. If `?` returns an error, roll back
    }
    DropGuard::dismiss(nums);  // ← 3. Parsing successful, dismiss the guard
    Ok(())
}
Conjuring zero-sized types
As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this.
This question is answered in Rust 1.100 with a single function: std::mem::conjure_zst.
Instead of transmuting (), MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init(), or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing.
Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's Python<'py> is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition.
Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo
Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds.
Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every bin in a package when only some may use it.
Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g.
warning: unused dependency `tracing-subscriber`
  --> Cargo.toml:23:1
   |
23 | tracing-subscriber.workspace = true
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default
help: consider removing the dependency on `tracing-subscriber`
A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table.
For example, running cargo check --bin foo won't show warnings for unused [dependencies] because another bin may be present that uses them.
No warning will be shown for unused dev-dependencies because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built.
This warning is being introduced as part of a new linting system for Cargo, controlled by the [lints.cargo] table in Cargo.toml, completing this project goal. See also the other lints that have been introduced.
Reducing Cargo cache collisions
Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the build-dir and then uplifts final artifacts to the target-dir. At this time, these share a common parent directory.
Different build configurations, like --features, can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the build-dir.
These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints.
This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on.
These problems get exacerbated when sharing a build-dir across git worktrees.
The build-dir now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory.
This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal, unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking.
We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases.
Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns
Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns.
You can opt in via .cargo/config.toml:
[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "3 days"
When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back:
$ cargo update
    Updating crates.io index
     Locking 2 packages to highest compatible version as of min-publish-age
      Adding cc v1.11.0 (available: v1.18.0, published 3 hours ago)
      Adding clap 4.6.7 (available: 4.6.9, published 2 days ago)
When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update:
$ CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE=allow cargo update clap --precise 4.6.9
    Updating crates.io index
    Updating clap 4.6.7 -> clap 4.6.9 (published 2 days ago, minimum age 3 days)
The newer version will be recorded in Cargo.lock and kept from then on until a later cargo update re-resolves it.
A few things to keep in mind:
- This depends on the registry recording when each version was published.
Versions without a pubtime field in the index are never held back.
- cargo install ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies.
Pin a version with cargo install foo@1.2.3 if needed.
- Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would.
Further work to protect the ecosystem is planned under the crates.io supply chain hardening project goal, including quarantine support and automated detection of suspicious releases.
Stabilized APIs
Other changes
Check out everything that changed in Rust, Cargo, and Clippy.
Contributors to 1.100.0
Many people came together to create Rust 1.100.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!

Libraries
- Stabilize custom allocators
- Map ENOTSUP to ErrorKind::Unsupported
- Fix soundness issues in std::sys::pal::sgx::waitqueue::unsafe_list
Stabilized APIs
Cargo
- Introduced Cargo's own linting system: some Cargo warnings are now emitted as lints that users can control in the [lints.cargo] table. This includes a new built-in unused dependency check via the cargo::unused_dependencies lint. docs #17298
- Introduced minimum publish age configurations, also known as dependency cooldowns. When the relevant config is set, the resolver ignores versions published more recently than that, unless they are already in Cargo.lock. (RFC 3923) docs #17335
- cargo-install: now uses the existing lockfile in the .crate tarball by default. --locked in cargo install becomes a no-op. #17388
- Cargo now uses a new directory layout for intermediate build artifacts. Tools that inspect the build directory may need to use Cargo’s JSON messages to locate build artifacts instead of relying on the build directory layout. The layout is not a stable interface and is subject to change. (build cache doc) #17354
Rustdoc
Compatibility Notes
- Closures now more precisely capture variables used in if let. This may cause new errors
- Check dyn-compatibility of trait objects in more places
- Infallible is now a type alias to !
- The never type fallback was changed to ! on all editions
- box patterns are no longer syntactically allowed
- Report Query Cycle errors in more cases when computing the layout of enums with explicit discriminants
- Always escape grapheme extenders in str::escape_debug
- Make let-else respect macro_rules expr metavariable grouping
- Iterator::{min,max}(_by_key) changed which Ord methods they use. This cannot change behaviour (other than being potentially faster) for types correctly following the Ord rules, but may impact types with inconsistent trait implementations.
- Emit an error when trying to enable SSE/AVX on an x86 (32bit or 64bit) softfloat target
- Require windowed (and exception) for Xtensa ABI
- windows-gnullvm: always link libunwind statically
- From version 1.94 up to 1.100 a number of ARMv7-A hardfloat targets required the VFPv3-D32 FPU as a minimum, as they erroneously had the d32 feature in their baseline list of features. Breakage introduced as a result of correcting this can be fixed by passing -Ctarget-feature=+d32 to Rust.
- Change "Rust" ABI on x86 to use SSE registers if they are always-available for the current target
- Make the ambiguous_glob_imported_traits lint fire in slightly more cases
- Make +fix-cortex-a53-835769 a default feature for aarch64-unknown-fuchsia
- Some impls on Box have been generalised to arbitrary allocators, which may cause new type inference errors
- The standard library now uses Unicode version 18.0.0
- WASI SDK version was bumped from 33 to 34
- On ARM targets, -Ctarget-feature/-Ctarget-cpu values that would alter the ABI are rejected as hard errors now.
